summary: This document directed IANA to allocate an IPv6 prefix for use with the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), to serve as endpoint identifier address space for sites deploying LISP. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This set aside a special range of internet addresses for an experimental system that separates who a computer is from where it is. The range is now only of historical interest.

questions: what is the lisp eid block
subtitle: An IPv6 address space set aside for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol

tldr.problem: LISP is an experimental protocol that separates the identity of a computer from its location, but LISP adopters need a dedicated address block for endpoint identifiers to enable experimentation without fragmenting their own addressing space.
tldr.mechanism: IANA allocates a /32 IPv6 prefix (2001:5::/32) reserved exclusively for LISP endpoint identifier space, with a hierarchical allocation framework allowing organizations to request and temporarily use sub-prefixes for LISP experiments.
tldr.outcome: LISP sites can deploy the protocol using a dedicated experimental address block, avoiding BGP routing table inflation and enabling faster LISP destination detection. The allocation was temporary (September 2016 to September 2019, extendable to 2022), and is now historic.

today: RFC 7954 is Historic. The IPv6 EID block allocation expired in September 2019 and was not made permanent. It is now returned to the free pool.

sections.title: What is LISP and Why a Special Address Block
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) is an experimental protocol that fundamentally changes how IP addressing works by separating the Endpoint Identifier (EID) space—which identifies who a computer is—from the Routing Locator (RLOC) space—which identifies where a computer is located in the network. This separation enables more flexible routing and allows computers to move across networks without changing their identity.

RFC 7954 directs IANA to allocate a /32 IPv6 prefix specifically for use as global LISP endpoint identifier space. This dedicated block enables organizations deploying LISP to use a reserved address range for their EID space, rather than using their own globally allocated unicast addresses. The block is used in conjunction with LISP mapping systems that track where each EID is located in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP is a new way to think about internet addresses: instead of one address meaning both 'who you are' and 'where you are', LISP separates them. This RFC set aside special addresses just for the 'who you are' part when testing LISP.

sections.title: Why LISP Adopters Need a Dedicated Block
sections.content:
LISP adoption brings several technical benefits that are enabled by having a dedicated EID block. Early LISP detection allows routers to quickly determine whether a destination is a LISP site without performing expensive lookups. Without a dedicated block, routers must cache lookups or send map requests to discover this information. Traffic engineering becomes easier because LISP and non-LISP traffic can be identified and treated differently based on the destination address alone, without inspecting the packet payload.

A dedicated block also helps with transition mechanisms and reduces impact on BGP routing. Organizations wanting to deploy LISP can request a prefix in the EID block and use it internally without announcing it in the public internet routing system, avoiding fragmentation of their own addressing space. If each LISP adopter instead used their own allocated addresses, the public routing table would suffer from increased fragmentation. Instead, a few Proxy Tunnel Routers (PxTRs) can announce large aggregates of the EID block to route traffic to LISP sites, reducing routing table inflation.
sections.plainLanguage: Having a special address block for LISP helps routers recognize LISP traffic quickly, lets people organize LISP traffic differently, and keeps the internet routing system from getting too bloated.

sections.title: The IPv6 Allocation
sections.content:
IANA allocated the /32 IPv6 prefix 2001:5::/32 for use as the global EID space for LISP. A /32 prefix is sufficiently large for the initial LISP experimentation phase. To provide context, the LISP Beta Network (which existed before this formal allocation) was already using a /32 prefix to serve more than 250 sites with /48 sub-prefixes, demonstrating that this block size could support significant deployment. A /32 is also comparable to previous tunneling protocol allocations like those in RFC 3056.

The allocation includes properties specifying that the block can be used as both a source and destination address, is forwardable, has global scope, and is reserved for use as EID space by LISP-enabled routers. The RFC specifies that this address space must be used only at the configuration level within LISP networks and must not be hard-coded into router hardware, to avoid locking out organizations that want to deploy LISP with their own existing prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: The special range is 2001:5::/32, which is big enough for thousands of organizations to each get their own smaller piece. It is marked in the global registry as reserved for LISP.

sections.title: The 3+3 Allocation Plan
sections.content:
IANA allocated the /32 prefix for an initial period of three years (September 2016 through September 2019) with an option to extend by three additional years (through September 2022). This time-limited approach was intentional: by the end of the first period, the IETF would evaluate whether LISP had sufficient technical benefits to warrant a permanent allocation.

If the IETF decided to make the allocation permanent, the block would be extended through September 2022 to allow time for the IETF to define the final size of a permanent EID block and create a transition plan. If the IETF did not see sufficient value, the entire /32 would be returned to the free address pool by September 2019. This experimental approach follows RFC 3692 guidelines for assigning experimental and testing numbers, with the important difference that the EID block provides globally unique addresses suitable for real interoperation, unlike purely private-use address ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA gave out the addresses for three years to test whether LISP would work well. After three years, they would decide if it was worth keeping the addresses for LISP permanently or giving them back.

sections.title: How LISP Sites Connect to the Internet
sections.content:
Organizations deploying LISP use prefixes from the EID block internally for their endpoint identifiers. Mappings that relate EID prefixes to their locations (RLOCs) are registered with one or more Map-Server entities and made available through the LISP mapping system.

For connectivity between LISP sites and the legacy Internet, Proxy Ingress Tunnel Routers (PITRs) can announce large aggregates (potentially just one large aggregate) of the IPv6 EID block. This allows routers on the legacy Internet to route traffic destined for LISP sites to a PITR, which encapsulates and forwards the traffic to the destination LISP site. Within a LISP site, not all routers need to run LISP; only border routers need LISP functionality. Routers used only for intra-domain routing can treat EID addresses like any other addresses and do not need any special LISP configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP sites mark their addresses with the special range and sign them up in a mapping service. Border routers from LISP sites can announce the whole block to the internet, so traffic gets routed to them correctly.
